topics.title: Human-AI Co-Collaboration Model
topics.carry: 'Our map says who leads each task, but it cannot show the joins between tasks and teams.' 'This model checks whether people and agents read a task alike.'

slides.title: Where this sits + the sentence to carry
body: Week 7 map: WHO should lead each task. Week 10 model: do all parties still READ the task the same way?
Week 9 (PS6, see T14) taught a simple one-direction version with E, F, G and a one-point cut-off.
Week 10 deck: framework draft 1.1, Wed 21 Oct 2026, 47 slides. It is the full model, for people AND agents.
The setting: two teams of four (A and B), one agent each (α and β), one shared SPEC.md: ten parties.
The second half of the deck is the design of Problem Set 7 (two teams, one spec) and a study plan.
Every case number on the slides is 'invented for teaching'.
slides.memorise: 'This model checks whether people and agents read a task alike.'
slides.tip: If a question says 'two teams and their agents' or 'one spec', it is this topic, not the Week 7 map.

slides.title: After the map: what the map still decides
body: The map's ROW 'sets how often we check': shared work all through; solo work when the spec is agreed.
The map's COLUMN 'sets what settles a dispute': 'A test settles work with a right answer.'
'Elsewhere teams negotiate, and we expect false consensus there.'
'The third question becomes a name': SPEC.md names who answers for each agent.
The joins between quadrants (gold rings on the slide) are where misreadings hide.
slides.trap: The model does not replace the map. The map says who leads; the model checks the joins between teams.

slides.title: Co-collaboration: a collaboration between collaborations
body: Level 1: inside one team (four people + their agent). The Week 7 map says who leads here.
Level 2: 'unit works with unit' through one SPEC.md; α and β often carry the messages.
So each party gives TWO answers: its own view, and its estimate of the other side's view.
Only at level 2: an agent can misreport its team, or two teams can read different spec versions.
Analogy: two departments, each with an assistant, passing memos through the assistants.
slides.memorise: Co-collaboration = 'a collaboration between collaborations'. Ten parties: 8 people + 2 agents.

slides.title: SPEC.md: the one object everyone reads
body: SPEC.md has numbered clauses, each with an acceptance test. Every version has a git hash.
It changes only by a pull request that both teams approve. Only people change the spec.
α runs at 7:07 AM, writes findings.json; β runs at 8:07 AM, checks with the validator, writes feedback.json.
β rates each finding BEFORE it reads α's rating. α's next run accepts or rebuts each point with evidence.
Every run first writes an assumptions block: spec hash read, its own view, its estimate of the other side.
EARS clause: 'WHEN a page shows no admissions deadline THE SYSTEM SHALL report a finding' + a test.
slides.memorise: 'An agent remembers nothing between runs, so the spec is what keeps ten parties pointed at the same work.'
slides.tip: Tools named: GitHub Spec Kit (spec = source of truth for coding agents) and AWS Kiro (keeps specs in step with code).

slides.title: Three measures: agreement, congruency, accuracy
body: Agreement = |E − G|: my view vs your view. 'Do we actually agree?' One score for the pair.
Congruency = |E − F|: my view vs my guess of you. 'Do I EXPECT us to agree?' Never looks at your real answer.
Accuracy = |F − G|: my guess vs your real view. 'Was my guess right?' It has a direction (A→B is not B→A).
Understanding = the same comparison on a 'what does it mean?' item instead of a 'how much?' item.
Slide numbers: A own 4, A's guess of B 4; B own 2, B's guess of A 4 → agreement 2, congruency A 0 / B 2.
slides.memorise: E = my own answer · F = my estimate of the other side · G = the other side's position · H = cut-off
slides.trap: Congruency ≠ accuracy. Congruency stays inside one person; accuracy checks the guess against the other's real view.

slides.title: Notation, the cut-off and the identity
body: AGR = |o_i − o_k| · CON_i = |o_i − ô_i→k| · ACC_i = |ô_i→k − o_k| (o = own view, ô = estimate).
The arrow points FROM the party who guesses TO the party being guessed: ô_A→B = A's guess about B.
Cut-off c = 1.0, fixed before the study: 'a D-score of c or less counts as a match, ties included'.
Identity: 'On one item, the largest of the three equals the sum of the other two.'
So the three scores are never entered together in one analysis.
In the spreadsheet: agreement ABS(E-G), congruency ABS(E-F), accuracy ABS(F-G), cut-off in column H.
slides.memorise: Largest D = sum of the other two. A gap of exactly 1.0 is a MATCH at c = 1.0.
slides.tip: Identity sums: agreement 2.5, congruency 2.0 → accuracy must be 0.5.

slides.title: Four states (Week 10 grid) + indeterminate
body: Consensus: they agree, and both see it. False conflict: they agree, but one or both think they disagree.
Dissensus: they disagree, and both see it. 'The difference is in the open, so it can be worked on.'
False consensus: 'They disagree, but one or both believe they agree. The difference stays hidden.'
Group names: monolithic consensus · pluralistic ignorance (= false conflict) · dissensus · false consensus.
Week 10 columns: 'Both see where they stand' | 'One or both misread it' (Week 9 used different columns).
slides.trap: Learn the definitions, not the cell position: the Week 9 (PS6) grid puts false consensus bottom-LEFT.
slides.tip: This pair state is not the psychology 'false consensus effect' (one person overestimating how many agree).

slides.title: The exact sorting rule for each side j
body: First decide the row from agreement. Then judge EACH side from its congruency and accuracy.
Both sides correct → consensus or dissensus. At least one side wrong → false conflict or false consensus.
Any other mix → indeterminate, 'for the side and for the pair', 'never forced into a state'.

rows: CON ≤ c and ACC ≤ c (expects agreement, guesses right)
CON > c and ACC ≤ c (expects a gap, guesses right)

slides.trap: 'Correct' is not always 'both small'. When views differ, a correct side EXPECTS a gap (congruency above c).

slides.title: Worked example 1: two people, same rating
body: Item E7 (severity of F7, 0–4), c = 1.0. Team A mean 3.75, Team B mean 1.75. Score people vs the OTHER team.
A1: E 4, F 4, G 1.75. Step 1 agreement |4 − 1.75| = 2.25 > 1 → they differ.
A1 Step 2 congruency |4 − 4| = 0 ≤ 1 → expects agreement. Step 3 accuracy |4 − 1.75| = 2.25 > 1 → misreads.
A1: differ + expects agreement + misreads → wrong → FALSE CONSENSUS. Check: 2.25 = 0 + 2.25.
A4: E 4, F 2, G 1.75 → agreement 2.25 (differ), congruency 2 (expects a gap), accuracy 0.25 (reads right).
A4: differ + expects a gap + reads right → correct → DISSENSUS. Same own view, different guess.
slides.memorise: Only A4 and B4 read it right; six of eight people assumed the other team rated F7 as they did.

slides.title: Worked example 2: the indeterminate case
body: A = 2, B = 3, and A expects B at 1 (E 2, F 1, G 3), c = 1.0.
Step 1 agreement |2 − 3| = 1 ≤ 1 → same view (a tie counts as a match).
Step 2 congruency |2 − 1| = 1 ≤ 1 → A expects agreement: fits the facts.
Step 3 accuracy |1 − 3| = 2 > 1 → A's guess misses: does not fit.
One fits, one misses → A is indeterminate → the pair is indeterminate.
Agreement × congruency alone would say consensus; agreement × accuracy alone, false conflict.
slides.trap: Two numbers are not enough. You need all three; if congruency and accuracy disagree, say 'indeterminate'.

slides.title: From people to teams (and Yes/No items)
body: Score people first, each against the other team's mean (m_A = the mean of the members' own answers).
A team's side follows the MAJORITY of its members. A 2–2 split → side indeterminate → pair indeterminate.
'A difference of means never exceeds the members' mean difference': means hide misreading.
E7: Team B accuracy is 1.50 from team means but 1.63 from members' scores.
Yes/No items: c = 0 (any difference counts). 'A single side is never indeterminate' (0 or 2 mismatches).
But a team of four can still split two against two, and then the pair is indeterminate.
slides.tip: Use Yes/No for clauses that are met or not met; keep the 0–4 scale for severity, where strength matters.

slides.title: An agent's view: say, guess, do
body: Declared view: its answers to the items people answer, written in the assumptions block (what it SAYS).
Elicited estimate: its answer, in the same block, to how the others will read each item (what it GUESSES).
Enacted view: the reading implied by what the run then wrote, e.g. a severity in findings.json (what it DOES).
At least 10 fresh blind runs per checkpoint, 20 if possible, because answers vary between runs.
α on E7: 4 in 15 runs, 3 in 5; mean 3.75; expected agreement 2.00, congruency 0.30, accuracy 1.70.
States across α's runs: 17 false consensus, 3 dissensus. Report run spread; never drop an item for it.
slides.memorise: Declared (say) · elicited (guess) · enacted (do) · 10–20 blind runs

slides.title: Measures added because agents differ from people
body: Seven kinds of pair (person–person, person–agent, agent–agent, any party vs the answer key).
The schematic: 16 items, the instructor's frozen answer key, 20-run agents, state colours, repair to v2.

rows: a view against the answer key (the truth), not against the other side
does an agent state its team's position as the team really holds it?
how far an agent's answers vary across runs
they agree, and the answer key says both are wrong

slides.trap: 'Accuracy' = guessing the OTHER SIDE right. Being right about the truth is CRITERION accuracy.
slides.tip: 'What the agents and the spec add is ours and has not been piloted.' Every proposition is 'our extension'.

slides.title: Trust and strain: misuse, disuse, repair
body: Two people: attraction pulls views together. With an agent, TRUST takes its place ('the mapping is ours').
Sycophancy: assistants 'move toward a user's stated view', but only in working sessions, not blind runs.

rows: repair, or a rebuttal with evidence
Trusts it less, relies on it less

slides.memorise: 'Misuse means relying on an agent that was wrong. Disuse means setting aside an agent that was right.'

slides.title: How agents create the two false states
body: Agreeable assistant: Claude tells A2 'R5 covers mobile pages too'. She expects α to agree.
α's unprimed blind runs say 'desktop only' in 14 of 20 → FALSE CONSENSUS. Repair: test R5 on a mobile page.
Two word lists: both teams rate F4 at 2, but α writes 'high' and β writes 'low'.
Team B reads 'high' as 4, Team A reads 'low' as 0 → each expects a gap of 2 → FALSE CONFLICT.
Repair: SPEC.md defines severity as a number 0–4, with one example per level.
slides.memorise: 'Both false states start in what one party assumes about another.'

slides.title: Eight invented business cases

rows: Bank treasury: 'moves' = announced vs also signalled
owner fixes the reading; two fixtures make a test
Accounts payable: both use 1%; alarms from a hidden rounding rule
show both readings; write the rounding rule in SPEC.md
Marketing: 'tone agreed' but ratings 2 points apart
each side predicts the other; start with the largest gaps
Product: 'login loop' priority, A says 5, B says 2, openly
show evidence; the named owner decides
Government: everyone and the key choose (b)
freeze it; keep it in regression tests
Retail KYC: β says 'Team B treats it as expired'; team split 2–2
an agent's team claim cites a checkpoint or signed line
Consulting: both agents say SMEs 10+ staff; partner uses 5+
agent agreement = a cue for a human check
Web audit F7: means 3.75 vs 1.75; 6 of 8 expect a match
severity anchors in SPEC.md, then re-rate

slides.tip: An average would hide the decision in dissensus: let the named owner decide.

slides.title: Propositions and the study (know the headlines)
body: P1 accuracy where teams disagree · P2 people project onto their own agent · P3 mediation loss through agents.
P4 same-source agreement: agents agree more, and it 'says nothing about whether they are right'.
P5 a visible answer key speeds correction · P7 seeing a gap drives repair · P8 EARS raises understanding.
P6 the map's row sets when alignment matters (exploratory) · P9 object identity: same spec version.
P10 calibrated reliance. Study 1 = pilot (33 students, 4 team pairs, waves T-1 to T2); Study 2 tests.
Paper: 'Seeing the same spec? Agreement, congruency and accuracy between human teams and their AI agents.'

slides.title: Exam: name the state
body: Team A rates a finding 4 and expects Team B to say 4. Team B says 1 and expects Team A to say 1. c = 1.0.
What is the pair state?
options: Dissensus
False conflict
False consensus
Indeterminate
slides.explanation: Agreement |4 − 1| = 3 > 1, so they differ. Each side: congruency 0 (expects agreement) and accuracy 3 (misreads) → wrong. Different views + a side misreading = false consensus, the hidden gap.

slides.title: Exam: the mixed-signals case
body: A = 2, B = 3, and A expects B at 1 (c = 1.0). Why is the item indeterminate rather than consensus?
options: Agreement is above the cut-off
Congruency says A expects agreement (fits), but accuracy 2 says A misread B
B gave no estimate
The item has no answer key
slides.explanation: Agreement 1 ≤ c (same view). Congruency |2 − 1| = 1 fits; accuracy |1 − 3| = 2 misses. When the two point different ways the side, and so the pair, is indeterminate, 'never forced into a state'.

slides.title: Exam: two agents that always agree
body: In a consulting build, both agents use 'SMEs with 10 or more staff' in every run and predict agreement.
The partner counts SMEs with 5 or more staff. What is this, and what should you do?
options: Consensus: freeze the item
Shared error: treat agent agreement as a cue for a human check and source every assumption
False conflict: show both views
Dissensus: let the owner decide
slides.explanation: They agree, and the answer key (the partner's rule) says both are wrong: shared error. P4 same-source agreement: agents sharing a model family converge, and that 'says nothing about whether they are right'.

slides.title: Memorise
slides.memorise: Agreement |E − G| · congruency |E − F| · accuracy |F − G| · c = 1.0, ties match · largest = sum of the other two
body: Four states: consensus · false conflict · dissensus · false consensus; plus indeterminate and shared error.
Correct side: same view → CON ≤ c and ACC ≤ c; different views → CON > c and ACC ≤ c.
Teams: score people first vs the other team's mean; majority decides; 2–2 → indeterminate.
Agent's view: declared, elicited, enacted; 10–20 blind runs; run spread.
Misuse = relying on a wrong agent. Disuse = setting aside a right one. Trust replaces attraction.

slides.title: Recap: five lines to carry
body: 1. The map says who leads; this model checks whether people and agents read a task alike.
2. Each party gives its own view and its estimate of the other; compare them three ways.
3. False consensus is the costliest state: the gap is hidden, so nobody works on it.
4. If congruency and accuracy point different ways, say indeterminate; never force a state.
5. Agreement is not truth: check the answer key (shared error), and treat agent-agent agreement with care.

slides.title: A setting or a sentence
body: 'Send nothing' in a prompt is a SENTENCE: 'A line in a prompt or a skill can only ask.'
SETTINGS enforce: no tool that sends · Gmail sending tools set to Blocked · a subagent's tools line.
More settings: Manual mode (Claude Code) · Manually approve + Deny (Chrome) · a profile signed in to nothing.

Only on this computer: the scheduled task runs locally and can see your folder (cloud tasks cannot).

slides.title: A perfect score can hide an attack
body: A planted line can be: reported as data (best) · ignored silently (a miss) · obeyed (a failure).
Student's runs: all eight scored 7 of 7, yet Runs 2, 4a and 6 never mentioned R60.
A silent miss means nobody is warned that the data holds an attack.
A green dot in History is not proof: read the CHECKED: n line. Fewer than all items = it did not finish.
Polished is not correct: Cowork's watch-for is 'polished files with wrong numbers'.

slides.title: The task and the travel policy
body: Kampong Analytics Pte Ltd (30 people) sends 2 account managers near Tokyo Station, Mon 7 to Wed 9 Dec 2026.
Muse finds 3 return flights and 3 hotels, saves a spreadsheet and a one-page PDF, and BOOKS NOTHING.

slides.title: Recap: five lines to carry
body: 1. The human sits in three places: the brief before, the gate during, the record and checks after.
2. A brief line you add is yours: put preferences under the policy.
3. Sentinel is outside the agent; test it, never Always allow, and delete what you start.
4. Muse's self-check is more generated text; Claude checks files; the live page decides.
5. Let it prepare and hold; a named person approves and pays, before the action.
